newsitem.title: GERMANY: France, Germany launch EU reform drive.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany launch EU reform drive.

text.p: France and Germany launched a joint initiative to reform the European Union on Monday, calling for closer cooperation on police, justice, foreign affairs and defence, and a shakeup of EU institutions.

But a letter by President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl to fellow EU leaders ahead of Friday's summit in Dublin left key issues vague, and the two countries apparently failed to entirely bridge differences on a "stability pact" to strengthen a future single European currency.

Kohl told a news conference that Paris and Bonn wanted to make a joint proposal when EU finance ministers meet on Thursday to try to break the deadlock on a pact to prevent countries that join the euro from overspending.
But he said work was still going on, suggesting Paris had not entirely endorsed Bonn's demands for automatic hefty fines on governments that breach deficit limits.

On defence, they approved a joint strategy document which Chirac called a "historic step" and agreed France would go ahead with developing a new spy satellite next year which Germany would join a year later when it had overcome budget problems.

Kohl and Chirac said their letter aimed to push forward slow moving negotiations in the EU's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) by focusing on "urgent questions" to enable the conclusion of a new treaty next June in Amsterdam.

"We consider the areas of internal and external security as well as institutional reform are particularly relevant. If we do not achieve joint decisions in these areas, we will expose the whole construction of Europe to great danger and we will not meet our responsibility towards future generations," they said.

The aim is to make EU institutions more effective to cope with the entry of former communist central and east European countries in the coming decade, enlarging the Union eventually to up to 27 states.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette complained last Friday that a draft treaty produced by Ireland reflected the "mediocrity" of the IGC negotiations so far.

The 10-page letter, addressed to the EU's Irish presidency, called for new institutions to "reinforce the effectiveness, continuity, coherence, solidarity and visibility" of a common European foreign and security policy.

Under the plan, a foreign policy analysis and planning unit in Brussels would prepare joint actions, headed by a senior official "possessing the necessary political stature" who would represent EU foreign policy when joint actions were agreed.

But the letter offered two alternatives: appointing a full-time "Mr Foreign Policy", as sought by France, or giving the job to the secretary-general of the EU's Council of Ministers -- a little-known German bureaucrat.
While unanimity would remain the rule for setting foreign policy objectives at summit level, the implementation of such actions should be decided by qualified majority voting.
France and Germany advocated gradually bringing the Western European Union defence grouping into the European Union, so EU summits could give it orders -- something Britain opposes.

Kohl and Chirac also proposed the creation of a "European judicial area" through a gradual harmonisation of drugs and crime legislation, the development of the Europol police agency and a gradual move to qualified majority voting on internal security issues.

They called for a reform of the weighted voting system "to guarantee a representative balance of member states" but gave no details. They also said the number of European commissioners must be reduced and national parliaments more closely associated with EU decision-making.
